subject: ela
intro: On the SAT, 'Sentence Boundaries' questions test whether you can fix fragments, run-ons, and comma splices and choose correctly among periods, semicolons, and colons. A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb and a complete thought; two complete sentences cannot be joined by a comma alone (that is a comma splice).

items.prompt: Is this a comma splice? 'The storm passed, the sun came out.'

steps: Both 'The storm passed' and 'the sun came out' are complete sentences.
Joining them with only a comma is a comma splice.
So yes, it is a comma splice.
solution.answer: Yes; it is a comma splice.

items.prompt: Fix the comma splice: 'The storm passed, the sun came out.'

steps: Use a period or semicolon between two complete sentences.
So: 'The storm passed. The sun came out.' (or '...passed; the sun came out.')
solution.answer: 'The storm passed. The sun came out.' (or a semicolon)

items.prompt: A group of words missing a subject or verb (or a complete thought) is a ____.
Two complete sentences joined by only a comma is a comma ____.
Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation is a ____.
